articles.title: Jamie Dimon warns US savers about Washington’s ‘heroin’ effect — it could crush you. Here’s how his bank protects itself
articles.summary: Hint: It prepares for trouble before trouble arrives.
articles.body:
Moneywise and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue through links in the content below.

Washington has a way of making the economy feel good. But Jamie Dimon wants Americans to look at what's fueling the high.

Speaking at the Economic Club of Chicago earlier this month, the CEO of JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM) compared government spending to a powerful drug — one that can boost corporate profits while setting the stage for a painful aftermath.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

Gold has overtaken U.S. Treasuries as central banks' top reserve asset. Get Goldco's 2026 Precious Metals IRA Playbook for free

"We've got to remember about government spending: It's inflationary," he said (1). "It also does something which is unbelievable — makes you all feel good. It's like heroin. It drives your corporate profits."

For Americans watching their savings, that's a troubling combination. Businesses can report stronger earnings while the dollars you've worked to put away buy less at the grocery store, gas station and checkout counter.

Dimon explained how the money moves through the economy: "When governments spend a trillion dollars, that goes into spending, that goes into all your businesses. Machine tools, burgers, pools, homes."

"And then we all feel good because we're all making a lot of money," he said. "And it's a little bit of a false thing if it's inflationary, which it is."

Washington's borrowing habit gives that warning plenty of weight.

According to Treasury Department data (2), the U.S. government spent $7.40 trillion in fiscal 2026 while collecting $5.40 trillion in revenue, resulting in a deficit of $1.99 trillion — an increase of $217 billion from fiscal 2025.

Dimon made clear that his concern stretches beyond one administration's signature legislation.

"It wasn't the One Big Beautiful Bill, guys," he said. "We have been profligate now for years."

So how does America's biggest bank protect itself?

It prepares for trouble before trouble arrives.

"We prepare for low rates, high rates, stock price down 40%, credit spreads going up, bond rates at 8%, high yield at 15%," Dimon said. "And JPMorgan can handle all of that."

For everyday Americans, the inflationary pain Dimon warned about is already hitting home. U.S. consumer prices have climbed 29.8% (3) since the beginning of 2020, with energy prices soaring 53.5% (4) over the same period.

articles.title: Identity thieves don’t need your password anymore. Here are 6 new account takeover threats
articles.summary: Account takeover threats go beyond stolen passwords as criminals exploit session cookies, SIM swaps and MFA fatigue to bypass your login security.
articles.body: You may think of a stolen password as the main way someone gets into your account. But online criminals have learned that they do not always need to steal the password itself. They may hijack an active login session, convince you to approve a sign-in, take control of your phone number or use malware to collect information from your device. Passwords are still important. However, they are only one part of the security system protecting your identity. Here are six ways criminals may try to get around traditional password protection and the practical steps you can take to protect yourself. Join our CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Join us today, Saturday, Oct. 31, at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT. Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com. Missed this morning’s live class? Register at CyberGuyLive.com to watch the replay. YOUR BANK MAY STOP TEXTING YOU SIX-DIGIT CODES 1. Stolen login sessions When you sign in to a website, the service often creates a session that tells it you have already proved who you are. Your browser or app may keep that session active so you do not have to enter your password every few minutes. Criminals can sometimes steal the digital tokens or cookies associated with these sessions. If the service accepts the stolen information, an attacker may gain access without entering your password or completing another verification step. How to protect yourself: Review the devices and active sessions connected to your accounts. Sign out of anything you don't recognize and check for suspicious login activity. We've previously explained how to check for unfamiliar devices and remove them from your Apple, Google and Microsoft accounts. If you suspect unauthorized access, change your password using a trusted device and revoke other sessions when the service allows it. Remember that removing a device from an account list does not always terminate an active login session. 2. SIM swaps and phone account fraud Your phone number is often connected to email, banking, payment and social media accounts. Criminals may try to convince a mobile carrier to transfer your number to a SIM card or eSIM they control. If the transfer succeeds, they may receive calls and text messages intended for you, including certain account verification codes. A sudden loss of cellular service can be an early warning sign, especially when there is no known local outage. Other signs include an unexpected carrier notification about a device change or a password-reset message you did not request. How to protect yourself: Ask your carrier about an account security PIN, number transfer lock and port-out protection. These protections vary by carrier. For sensitive accounts, use a passkey, security key or authenticator app when available. Unlike text verification codes, authenticator app codes generally do not depend on your phone number. If text messages are your only available second authentication method, keep them enabled. They still provide more protection than relying on a password alone. ARE BANK TEXT CODES ENOUGH TO PROTECT YOU? 3. Fake login approvals and MFA fatigue Multifactor authentication, or MFA, adds another layer of protection to your accounts. However, criminals sometimes target the person receiving the security request. One tactic is MFA fatigue, also called push bombing. An attacker who can trigger authentication requests repeatedly sends approval notifications, hoping you eventually tap "Approve" to make them stop. Criminals may also impersonate technical support or a financial institution and ask you to read aloud a one-time security code. How to protect yourself: Never approve a login you did not initiate or share a verification code with someone who unexpectedly contacts you. If repeated prompts appear, deny them and check the account through its official website or app. Change your password if you suspect it has been compromised. When available, choose phishing-resistant authentication, such as a passkey or security key. App-based approvals that require number matching can also offer additional protection against accidental approvals. 4. Malware and risky browser extensions An infostealer is malicious software designed to collect information from a device. Depending on its capabilities, it may steal browser-stored passwords, session cookies, payment information or other sensitive data. These programs can arrive through fake software updates, pirated applications, suspicious email attachments, malicious advertisements or compromised browser extensions. Some malware operates quietly, which means you may not immediately notice anything unusual. How to protect yourself: Keep your operating system, browser and security software updated. Avoid downloading software from unfamiliar websites and review browser extensions regularly. If you suspect malware has compromised a device, use a separate, trusted device to secure important accounts. Run a security scan with strong antivirus software and remove suspicious software. For a serious infection, professional assistance or reinstalling the operating system may be necessary. Avoid signing back into sensitive accounts until you are confident the device is secure. 5. Malicious apps with access to your accounts Some criminals do not need to steal your password or infect your device. Instead, they may trick you into giving a connected application permission to access your information. For example, a fake productivity tool might ask to read your email, access your contacts or manage files in your cloud storage. You may encounter a legitimate-looking permission screen asking you to approve those requests. If you grant access to a malicious app, it may be able to retrieve information through the permissions you approved. In certain cases, that access can continue even after you change your account password. This technique is sometimes called OAuth consent phishing. In a September 2026 warning, the FBI explained that criminals can trick people into granting malicious applications access to their accounts. That access can remain active even after a password change unless the victim revokes the application's permissions. How to protect yourself: Review the third-party applications connected to your Google, Microsoft and other important accounts. Look closely at what each application can access. Remove permissions for apps you no longer use or do not recognize. Be especially careful with applications requesting access to email, contacts, cloud files or account management features. Passkeys can help, but they are not the whole answer Passkeys can significantly reduce the risk of traditional password phishing. They use cryptographic credentials associated with your device, security key or password manager. Unlike a password that you type into a website, a properly implemented passkey is tied to the legitimate website or service. That makes it much harder for a fake login page to steal the credential. However, passkeys do not eliminate every security risk. Criminals may still target an already authenticated session, an infected device, a malicious connected application or an account recovery process. How to protect yourself: Use passkeys when your important accounts support them. Protect your devices with a strong screen lock and keep recovery information current. If a service offers backup recovery codes, store them securely so you can regain access if your primary device is lost or damaged. Why changing your password may not be enough Changing a compromised password is important, but it may not automatically remove every form of unauthorized access. Some services revoke existing sessions after a password change, while others require you to sign out of devices separately. A criminal might also have established another route into your account, such as an app-specific password, an unauthorized connected application or a new recovery method. Your email deserves particular attention. Someone with access to your inbox could create forwarding rules that quietly send copies of your messages elsewhere. Review security settings for unfamiliar recovery addresses, connected devices, forwarding rules and app permissions. Remove anything you did not authorize. Also, check whether your password was reused elsewhere. If it was, replace those passwords with unique credentials. A password manager can make this easier without requiring you to memorize every login. What to do if someone gets around your password If you suspect an account takeover, act quickly. Start with the account that controls access to your other accounts, usually your primary email. Here's where to focus: A credit freeze is free and can help prevent criminals from opening new credit accounts in your name. You must contact all three major credit bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, to freeze your reports at each bureau. If you believe someone has stolen your identity, visit IdentityTheft.gov for a personalized recovery plan from the Federal Trade Commission. The value of watching beyond the login Strong account security is essential, but identity misuse can happen outside the original account. A criminal might use exposed personal information to apply for credit, take over a mobile account or attempt financial fraud without triggering a traditional password alert. That's where an identity theft protection service can provide another layer of monitoring. These services can monitor certain financial accounts, credit activity and exposed personal information for signs of suspicious activity. Some also provide identity restoration specialists who can help you navigate the recovery process if your identity is stolen. Features vary by provider and plan, and no service can prevent every form of identity theft. For additional peace of mind, consider a service that offers monitoring, timely alerts and recovery assistance. See my picks for the best identity theft protection services at Cyberguy.com to compare your options and find the right coverage for your needs. Pro tip: Protect the accounts that unlock everything else Once a month, review active sessions for your main email and financial accounts. Remove devices you no longer use and check whether your recovery information or connected app permissions have changed. Pay attention to unexpected login alerts, changes to your mobile account and new financial activity. A short monthly security check can help you spot suspicious changes before they become a larger problem. FAKE CHROME UPDATE SCAM COULD INFECT YOUR COMPUTER Kurt's key takeaways For years, I've told people to use strong passwords and turn on two-factor authentication. I still stand by that advice. But what concerns me now is how criminals can get into accounts without ever knowing the password. Think about someone quietly reading your email through a connected app you forgot about or using a stolen login session to access information you've worked hard to protect. You might change your password and assume everything is fine, while that access remains open. That's why I recommend checking which devices and apps have access to your most important accounts. Start with email and your mobile carrier, because losing control of either can create problems with your financial accounts. And while identity theft monitoring services can help alert you to certain suspicious activity, they work best alongside strong account security. A few minutes reviewing your settings today could save you a great deal of trouble later. Have you ever received a login approval or password-reset request you didn't initiate, and did you take action or ignore it? articles.title: Binance recovers 90 percent of stolen assets from hack
articles.summary: Cryptocurrency exchange Binance said Saturday that it was able to replenish 90 percent of the stolen assets ‌after a $6.3 billion hack of its platform. On Thursday, the money started moving out of Binance wallets, prompting the company to suspend all deposits and withdrawals. Some cryptocurrency firms froze around $3 billion in assets in connection…
articles.body:
Cryptocurrency exchange Binance said Saturday that it was able to replenish 90 percent of the stolen assets ‌after a $6.3 billion hack of its platform.

On Thursday, the money started moving out of Binance wallets, prompting the company to suspend all deposits and withdrawals. Some cryptocurrency firms froze around $3 billion in assets in connection with the incident.

“All BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC are fully backed 100%,” the company said in post on social platform X on Saturday. “We will continue to buy the remaining relevant token assets through market and OTC channels until the covered amount reaches 100% for all tokens.”

The company also said it will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not the users. In a previous update , Binance said it had set aside $6.34B in company funds to cover hacked losses.

President Trump said Friday that the administration is looking into the incident. When asked if the hack should be attributed to a suspected North Korean hacker group, the president said, “we don’t know.”

According to two blockchain intelligence firms, TRM Labs and Chainalysis, a North Korea-based cybercrime group TraderTraitor appeared to be behind the hacking incident. TRM Labs also noted that several aspects of the latest hack matched earlier North Korea-linked incidents like the $1.5 billion hack of crypto exchange Bybit last year.

In its Saturday update, Binance said after the 90 percent replenishment, the remaining 10 percent consists of “assets are less liquid, which means they may take longer to source in the required amounts.”

The company said the replenishment came from a partial deployment of the Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a portion of its Futures insurance fund and as well as Binance’s corporate treasury.
